chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Sahl, from Zakariyya ibn Adam, who said:

I asked al-Rida (peace be upon him) about a group of the enemy who made peace but then betrayed (or were unjustly treated), and perhaps they only betrayed because justice was not done to them. Is it permissible to buy from their captives? He said: 'If they are from the enemy whose enmity has become clear, then buy from them; and if they have departed and were treated unjustly, then do not buy from their captives.'

And with this chain of narration, he said: I asked him about the captives of the Daylam, some of whom steal from others, and the Muslims raid them without an Imam. Is their purchase permissible? He said: 'When they acknowledge servitude, there is no harm in buying them.'
ai.seo_question: What is the condition for purchasing captives from enemies who were treated unjustly or are known for internal theft?
ai.summary: Imam al-Rida (peace be upon him) establishes a jurisprudential criterion for purchasing war captives based on the clarity of their enmity versus the justice of their treatment, ruling that those wrongfully taken should not be bought. This distinction highlights the Shia emphasis on equitable conduct in *jihād* and the legal status of *mukātaba* (manumission agreements), as seen in the permissibility of buying Daylam captives who acknowledge servitude despite internal discord.
